messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amara Okafor, a 35-year-old tutor, was raped three years ago by the father of a child she was tutoring after an evening session. The assault happened while the toddler cried in the next room, a sound she could not drown out. She had felt a sudden wave of nausea as he pressed her down, and the entire situation had unfolded in a blur of uncertainty—she had not seen it coming, had not registered any threat until it was too late. The rape itself felt unreal, as if she were floating above her own body, watching someone else being hurt. Now, when she tries to talk about it, her throat closes. She can only describe the terror that surges back whole, but the event itself remains beyond words, like a locked room she can’t enter.

In the months afterward, Amara began to notice that certain sounds would hit her like a physical blow. A child crying on the street, or even in a grocery store, would make her stomach lurch and her mind instantly fill with the appraisal that she was permanently damaged—that the rape had changed her for the worse and she would never be whole again. The same feeling washed over her whenever something felt uncertain, like an unexpected change in her tutoring schedule, or when she felt queasy for any reason. That nausea became a trigger in itself, and each time her stomach turned, she believed even more firmly that she could not handle even the slightest upset. She had come to think that if she allowed herself to truly remember the event, she would shatter, so she tried to keep her mind strictly on the present, but the memory kept intruding—alien, belonging to someone else, yet bringing back the exact same terror. Those intrusions made her even more convinced that she was fundamentally broken.

To manage, Amara developed a set of strategies that she believed were keeping her safe. She started turning down invitations to social gatherings or date nights with her partner, Derek, because those were situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful—and she was certain that a good feeling would only be snatched away, leaving her more fragile. She also avoided any conversation where someone might bring up her assault; she would change the topic or leave the room if a friend mentioned the word “trauma” or even alluded to violence. But these avoidances came with a cost. By dodging positive events, she spent more time alone, ruminating on why she had not fought back, why she had not seen it coming. That self-blame loop made the memory feel more vivid and more alien at the same time, as if she were rehearsing a scene from someone else’s life. Her avoidance of reminders also backfired: the more she steered clear of children’s crying, the more acutely she heard it when it did occur, and the more her stomach churned, confirming that she could not cope.

At work, Amara now only tutors adults, having quietly stopped taking on families with young children. She keeps her schedule rigid to avoid any uncertainty—no last-minute changes, no unexpected cancellations. Even a student’s sigh can trigger a wave of nausea and the thought that she is permanently ruined. The self‑blame rumination has become a nightly ritual: she replays the event, berating herself, and each time the memory feels less like her own, yet the terror remains undiminished. She has started to believe that thinking about the assault at all would be impossible to survive, so she tries to clamp down on the images, but they break through anyway. Her partner, Derek, has noticed that she flinches when he touches her unexpectedly, and she has pulled away from the few positive interactions that once brought her joy. He eventually convinced her to seek help after she canceled a weekend trip they had planned—a trip she admitted she was avoiding because feeling happy seemed dangerous.

What finally brought Amara to the clinic was not her own sense of suffering but the realization that she was disappearing from her own life. She is terrified that she will never feel normal again, that the damage is permanent, and that no amount of talking will ever put the events into words. But she is even more afraid that if she does begin to remember fully, she will not survive the weight of it.
